definition: Brain.js is a JavaScript library used for neural networking, which is released as free and open-source software under the MIT License.
details: It can be used in both the browser and Node.js backends. Brain.js is most commonly used as a simple introduction to neural networking, as it hides complex mathematics and has a familiar modern JavaScript syntax. It is maintained by members of the Brain.js organization and open-source contributors.

explainer.lead: Brain.js is a free, open-source JavaScript library for building and using neural networks in web browsers or Node.js. Its familiar JavaScript syntax and hidden mathematical complexity make it especially approachable for people taking their first steps with neural networks.

tiers.eli5: Brain.js is like a ready-made building kit for teaching a computer to spot patterns. You give it examples using JavaScript, and it adjusts a small learning system so it can make guesses about new examples. It works both on web pages and on computers running JavaScript behind the scenes.
tiers.practitioner: Use Brain.js when a JavaScript browser application or Node.js backend needs a comparatively simple neural-network workflow without exposing the underlying mathematics. Prepare representative examples, train the network, and check its predictions on examples not used for training. Hiding the mathematics simplifies the code, but it does not remove the need to choose suitable data, settings, and evaluation checks.
tiers.paperLevel: Brain.js is a software library rather than a neural-network model or learning algorithm. In general notation, a neural network computes y = f(x; theta), where x is an input and theta contains adjustable parameters; training changes theta to reduce error on examples. Brain.js wraps this kind of workflow in JavaScript for browser and Node.js environments, with an emphasis on accessibility rather than exposing the underlying mathematics.

explainer.example: A beginner could write a browser-based JavaScript exercise that gives Brain.js several small input patterns paired with desired outputs. After training, the page could supply a new pattern and display the network's predicted output, letting the learner compare it with the expected answer.

usedIn.name: Neural-network education
usedIn.detail: A simple way to introduce neural-network ideas through familiar JavaScript syntax.

usedIn.name: Browser applications
usedIn.detail: Neural-network code can run directly in JavaScript-based web pages.

usedIn.name: Node.js backends
usedIn.detail: The same library can be used in server-side JavaScript applications.

explainer.intuition: Brain.js supplies the neural-network machinery so you can focus on providing JavaScript data and asking for training or predictions. It is a toolkit for learning patterns, not a pre-trained system with knowledge of its own.
howItWorks: Write JavaScript that runs in either a browser or a Node.js backend.
Provide example inputs and the results the network should learn.
Let Brain.js handle the neural-network calculations during training.
Use the trained network to produce outputs for new inputs.
Check those outputs rather than assuming every prediction is correct.
explainer.whyItMatters: It lowers the entry barrier for JavaScript developers who want to experiment with neural networks without first working through all the mathematics. Its browser and Node.js support also keeps experiments within a familiar development environment.
misconceptions: Brain.js is a library, not a single pre-trained neural network.
Simple syntax does not guarantee good training data or accurate predictions.
Running in JavaScript does not limit it to browsers; it also works in Node.js.
